DLVH4's own highlight feature (StatementScreen's `highlightOrderId`, merged 2654a348) was verified only against a single, already-fully-loaded page (rider_inbox_history_test.dart's own highlight test constructs a StatementPage with hasMore:false and both entries already present) -- the pagination-boundary case the brief warns about was never actually exercised. Confirmed fresh by reading `statement_screen.dart` directly, not assumed from the test gap alone: `initState` calls `_loadMore()` exactly once; `EarningTile(..., highlighted: e.orderId == widget.highlightOrderId)` only ever highlights an entry already present in `_lines`; nothing checks whether the target was found, and nothing continues loading further pages automatically. A rider reached here via history's own "In a weekly statement" link (DLVH3/DLVH4) whose originating order happens to be beyond the first `statementPageSize` (50) entries of that week's statement sees an UNHIGHLIGHTED, seemingly-normal list, with a plain "Load more" button and no indication their own order is further down or that highlighting is even pending -- a silent gap, not an honest one. Confirmed this is safely BOUNDED, not a "download everything" case the brief separately warns against for full history: `statementLines` is scoped to one rider's one week (`riderId` + `statementId`), a realistic weekly delivery count even for a very active rider is a small, finite number of 50-row pages -- auto-continuing until found or exhausted is safe, unlike history's own unbounded, multi-year scope. SCOPE: `_loadMore()` gains a check after each successful page load -- if `highlightOrderId` is set, not yet present among `_lines`, and `_hasMore` is still true, it awaits another call to itself before returning, chaining through as many pages as it takes (bounded by the statement's own finite size) until the target is found, the data is exhausted (an honest, correctly-unhighlighted outcome if the id turns out not to belong to this statement at all), or a page fails (the existing retry button surfaces normally, no forced retry loop on failure). The existing single-page test's own assertions are unaffected -- auto-continue is a no-op whenever `highlightOrderId` is null (the other two ways this screen is reached) or already found on the first page. New tests: the target on a LATER page auto-loads through to it without any manual "Load more" tap; a target that never appears exhausts all pages honestly (ends unhighlighted, not stuck loading forever); a null `highlightOrderId` does not trigger any extra page loads beyond what the rider explicitly requests (no regression to the plain-pagination case). may_write: `apps/delivery/lib/screens/money/statement_screen.dart`, `apps/delivery/test/rider_inbox_history_test.dart`, this ledger row. must_not_touch: `rider_money.dart`'s `statementLines` (the query itself is correct and unchanged -- this is a client-side continuation policy, not a backend fix), every other screen. Confirmed by re-reading the actual current source, not assumed from the review's own wording: (1) `_loadMore()`'s `_lines.addAll(page.lines)` has NO deduplication at all -- unlike `RiderHistory`'s own established `_items.addAll(page.items.where((o) => !seen.contains(o.id)))` pattern in the SAME app, used precisely to guard against a race where new data shifts the pagination window between page loads. (2) DLVH8's own auto-continue recursion trusts the backend's `hasMore`/cursor completely -- nothing checks whether the cursor genuinely advances between calls, so a hypothetical backend anomaly returning the identical last document forever would recurse without bound; and nothing caps the total page count, so DLVH8's own claimed boundedness argument ('a realistic weekly delivery count') was an assumption about DATA, not a guarantee enforced in CODE. (3) once found, the highlighted `EarningTile` is correctly colored but the screen's body is a plain, uncontrolled `ListView` -- nothing scrolls it into the visible viewport, so a target beyond the first screenful would be technically present and correctly highlighted yet invisible without the rider manually scrolling past everything ahead of it, unaware there was anything to look for. SCOPE: (1) `_loadMore()` dedupes new lines against every `orderId` already in `_lines` before appending, mirroring `RiderHistory`'s own established convention exactly. (2) a page's own cursor id is compared against the PREVIOUS call's cursor id; if unchanged despite `hasMore` claiming otherwise, `_hasMore` is forced to false (treated as exhausted, not as an error surfaced to the rider -- an anomaly this defensive, if it ever occurred, is not something a rider could act on) rather than recursing on an unmoving page. (3) a hard cap on auto-continued pages (a count so far beyond any plausible real weekly statement that reaching it can only mean a genuine anomaly, not normal use) stops the automatic chain -- manual 'Load more' remains available beyond it, since `_hasMore` itself is untouched by the cap. (4) once the target is genuinely found in `_lines` (not merely exhausted-and-absent), a post-frame callback uses `Scrollable.ensureVisible` via an internal GlobalKey on that one row's subtree to bring it into view, once per screen instance (a guard flag prevents re-triggering on later, unrelated rebuilds). IFSC identifies a bank BRANCH, not an account; two different real customers at the same branch can and do share a last-4 digit sequence by pure coincidence. A legacy withdrawal (no destinationFull) whose seller changed to a DIFFERENT account that happens to share the same last-4+IFSC as the frozen masked destination would be classified legacyVerified and its FULL live account number shown to the admin as if proven correct -- a real regression that reintroduces a weaker version of the exact class of risk ADMR-77/78 exist to close, this time via a false positive rather than a stale read. Money-safety scope, verified precisely rather than assumed: markWithdrawalPaidCore (server) never reads this resolved full destination at all -- it only ever records the frozen masked `destination` field, unaffected by this bug -- so the SYSTEM's own paidTo record was never at risk; the actual risk is a human being shown the wrong real bank account number to manually wire real money to, which the system's own bookkeeping would not catch. Fix: destinationMatchesMasked is downgraded to a pure CONSISTENCY check (its own doc comment now says so explicitly) never sufficient on its own to grant a 'resolved' status; a new resolveLegacyDestinationFromHistory queries the seller's own seller_payout_change_requests (which store FULL unmasked account details at proposal time, confirmed by re-reading requestPayoutChangeCore/reviewPayoutChangeCore directly -- the same real provenance seller_payout_change_requests' own firestore.rules comment already calls out: 'holds the full new account number: owner + admin read only, like seller_payout_details') and resolves exactly one of two genuinely provable cases: (a) the most recent APPROVED change whose reviewedAt is at or before the withdrawal's own createdAt IS the real historical destination -- used only after its own masked shape is cross-checked for internal consistency against the withdrawal's frozen `destination`; (b) if NO approved change exists before OR after the withdrawal at all, the CURRENT live seller_payout_details is provably unchanged since request time (proven by the absence of any approval event, not by a masked-field coincidence) and is used directly. Every other case -- a change happened only AFTER the withdrawal with no earlier record to anchor to, or the found record's own masked shape does not match the withdrawal's frozen one -- resolves to a new, explicit legacyUnresolved state showing only the masked info with a clear explanation of the exact missing evidence, never a reconstructed guess. legacyVerified is removed as a label entirely, per the owner's own explicit instruction. Also verified, not assumed: whether the server itself needs a parallel gate against 'a direct call bypassing the UI' -- confirmed it does not, because markWithdrawalPaidCore never granted or denied anything based on this resolved-destination status in the first place (it was always, only, a client-side DISPLAY concern for the admin's own manual wire-transfer instructions -- the money-recording path itself was never gated by it), disclosed explicitly rather than silently assumed either way. Its own stated 'last observed develop: 413244a1' is stale -- develop had already advanced to 41a2640e via this session's own ADMR-86 (investigation-navigation UI) and ADMR-87 (the first live-browser operator-journey verification in this whole saga, plus a real App Check emulator-mode fix) before this prompt arrived; verified fresh via `git log -1 develop`, not assumed from the prompt's own stated checkpoint or from memory. SCOPE: prompt section 2's own critique verified TRUE against the actual merged source, not assumed: parseStatusCursor(v) returns undefined for BOTH v===undefined (a key genuinely absent) AND v===null (`!v` is true for both) -- financeReconciliation.ts's own ScanCursor OUTPUT uses `null` to mean 'this group is exhausted', so a client that takes a scan result's own nextCursor and passes it back verbatim as the next call's cursor input (exactly what finance_reconciliation_screen.dart's own _loadMore does: `cursor: _nextCursor`) has every already-exhausted group's `null` silently reinterpreted as 'absent' -> `undefined` -> boundedByStatus's own `if (startAfter)` check is false -> that group's query runs from the TOP again on every subsequent page. Confirmed by full read-through, not by running the buggy path (the fix supersedes it directly). Section 3's own precision critique verified empirically: `new Timestamp(1700000000, 123456789)`, `t.toMillis()` then `Timestamp.fromMillis(that)` round-trips to a DIFFERENT Timestamp (`t.isEqual(...)` false) -- toMillis() genuinely truncates sub-millisecond nanos, exactly the loss the prompt names. Fix: the cursor wire contract is redesigned around an explicit tagged state (`{state:'start'}` / `{state:'continue', cursor:{seconds,nanoseconds,id}}` / `{state:'exhausted'}`) instead of inferring meaning from JS null/undefined, which does not survive a callable's own JSON marshalling reliably in the first place -- that IS the root cause, not merely a missed null-check. StatusCursor stores seconds+nanoseconds (Firestore's own lossless representation) instead of a single lossy millisecond value. A cursor schema version is validated and rejected (not silently restarted) on mismatch; any other malformed cursor shape is rejected the same way, never silently treated as 'start'. This has ZERO backward-compatibility obligation: financeReconciliationScan/RecheckFinding have never been deployed to the live agrimore-66a4e project (confirmed: every phase from ADMR-80 through 87 states its own deploy consequence and the owner has not run any of them), so the wire contract can change cleanly. may_write: functions/src/admin/financeReconciliation.ts, functions/scripts/phaseADMR80_finance_reconciliation_test.js (r16/r17's own call sites use the old StatusCursor-direct shape and must be updated to the new GroupCursorState shape; new multi-group round-trip regression scenarios per section 4), apps/admin/lib/screens/admin/finance/finance_reconciliation_screen.dart (round-trips the new cursor shape opaquely -- stores and replays exactly what the server sent, never reconstructs or reinterprets it client-side), this ledger row, CHECKLIST.md. must_not_touch: evaluateWithdrawal's own detection logic, confirmation semantics, recheckFindingCore, the three financial LINK_RECORD_TYPES, financial_record_detail_screen.dart -- all already correct and unrelated to the cursor contract itself.
